prompt: Why can no network firewall stop web from reaching SSH on desk in this lab?

choices.text: Because desk's SSH server has no password set for the portal account
choices.why: Reaching the port has nothing to do with passwords.

choices.text: Because network firewalls only filter traffic to the internet
choices.why: They filter between any segments they sit between.

prompt: What is it called when an intruder on one compromised machine moves on to the next?

choices.text: Exfiltration

choices.text: Lateral movement

choices.text: Persistence

prompt: What does `meta skuid "portal"` match?

choices.text: Packets addressed to the portal's port
choices.why: Ports are dport; skuid is about the sender's account.

choices.text: Packets whose payload contains the word portal
choices.why: nftables does not read payloads for words.

choices.text: Every packet the portal service receives from nginx
choices.why: It matches outgoing packets by the socket's owner.

choices.text: Packets from sockets the portal account owns
choices.why: Right: a rule about the account is a rule about the program.

prompt: Why does the portal rule use reject rather than drop?

choices.text: On its own machine there is nobody to hide from, and an answer saves a timeout
choices.why: Right: silence protects from strangers, not from local programs.

choices.text: Because drop does not work on outgoing packets
choices.why: web_egress drops outgoing packets.

choices.text: To tell desk that the portal tried
choices.why: The packet never reaches desk.

choices.text: Because reject is counted and drop is not
choices.why: Both can carry a counter.

prompt: Two services run under the same account. What does that do to a rule written per account?

choices.text: Nothing, because nftables tells them apart by process
choices.why: skuid sees the account only.

choices.text: Both share it
choices.why: Right: one more reason for an account per service.

choices.text: The rule applies to whichever service started first
choices.why: It applies to every socket of the account.

choices.text: The rule fails to load until one of them is moved
choices.why: It loads; it just cannot tell the two apart.

choices.why: Priority has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because only root may name a service

choices.text: Because the table portal_out had not been created

prompt: After the probe ended, the listing showed a number where its path had been. What does that mean for a service that restarts?

choices.text: The rule must be reloaded after each start
choices.why: Right: a restart makes a new group, and the old number matches nothing.

choices.text: Nothing: nftables follows the service across restarts by its name
choices.why: It holds the group's identity, which changes.

choices.text: The rule now applies to every service on the machine
choices.why: It matches one old group, which no longer exists.

choices.text: The kernel deletes the rule along with the group
choices.why: The rule stayed, printed with a number.

prompt: How many rules in web_egress let traffic out, before the counter?
A drop rule's counter is still zero after six months. What is the right reaction?

choices.text: Delete it at once: it does nothing
choices.why: It may guard against something rare; ask first.

choices.why: Zero may also mean it no longer matches what it was written for.
